ours.name: South Ridge (Scatter Lake)
ours.approach: From Twisp, drive Twisp River Road west approximately 22-24 miles to the Scatter Creek/Scatter Lake trailhead (~3,100-3,200 ft), about 50 yards past the Slate Creek Trail junction sign. Follow the Twisp River Trail (#440) a few hundred feet to the Scatter Creek Trail (#427) and take it through timber alongside Scatter Creek for about 4.2-4.5 miles to alpine Scatter Lake (~7,047-7,100 ft).
ours.descent: Downclimb the gendarme band back along the south ridge, then descend the talus slope roughly 500 ft back to Scatter Lake. In dry summer/fall conditions many parties scree-ski or plunge-step the looser sections of the talus for a quick descent, then retrace the Scatter Creek Trail back to the trailhead.

fktText: Description Abernathy peak is a high point on Abernathy Ridge standing at 8,321 feet, just tall enough to make it on the Washington Bulger List (98/100). SummitPost describes the peak as "alpine and eroded...However, what it lacks in technical terrain, it makes up for in solitude, height, and views." Both Jason Hardrath ( IG ) and Alden Ryno ( IG ) agree that this peak boasts some of the greatest views in the Cascades, Ryno saying that it was near the top of his list for "effort to reward ratio." The views, coupled with the less-than-intimidating terrain and very runnable trail, makes this peak available to anyone who doesn't love the technical and chossy scrambling so common in the North Cascades. Getting there: The trailhead is located off of National Forest Road 4440, to the Northeast of Twisp, WA. NF-4440 is primarily gravel, but as of the time of this submission was easily passable for two-wheel-drive vehicles. Google Maps link to trailhead here . The route: Starting at the sign at the trailhead, follow the trail that leads to Scatter Lake. This well-used trail switchbacks up along the side of Scatter Creek, which is not easily accessible along the first few miles of trail. Eventually, the trail will lead you to a small basin. You'll see a large waterfall to climber's left and then you will climb steeply out of this lower basin to an upper basin. Scatter Lake is a vivid blue and very inviting on a hot day and you'll get your first views of Abernathy Peak. The trail skirt

ours.name: Northeast Couloir
ours.approach: From the Stuart Lake/Mountaineer Creek trailhead, follow the Stuart Lake Trail past the Colchuck Lake junction (do not turn off), then leave the trail to bushwhack and cross Mountaineer Creek (a notorious slide-alder slope is best avoided via nearby talus). Snow is typically encountered around 4,700 ft; continue to the base of the north face couloir.
ours.descent: Retrace your steps from the summit to the upper rock band, then make one rappel onto the ledge on the southeast face; you may need to rig a natural anchor, and one party used a slung tree there. Then head over to the top of the Northeast Couloir and find the gully just east of it: two or three single-rope rappels down that gully reach the snow slopes below. ours.name: West Ridge via Wildhorse Creek
ours.approach: From the Whitepine Creek Trailhead (about 2,800 ft), follow Whitepine Creek Trail #1582 up the valley for about 2.5 miles to the junction with Wildhorse Creek Trail #1592. Bear left onto the Wildhorse Creek Trail and climb through forest into the Wildhorse basin to about 5,400 ft, where the trail passes directly west of the summit. Leave the trail here.
ours.descent: Reverse the route: down the summit ledges to below the headwall, back west along the west ridge, then down through the meadows to rejoin the Wildhorse Creek Trail, and out the Whitepine Creek Trail to the car.

fktText: Description Big Chiwaukum is the high point of the Chiwaukum Mountains, tucked between the Enchantments and Stevens Pass – an alpine scramble with beautiful views, without the major crowds of its more famous neighbors. From the Whitepine Creek Trailhead (2,800 ft), follow Whitepine Creek Trail (#1582) approximately 2.7 miles to its junction with Wildhorse Creek Trail (#1592). Continue on Wildhorse Creek Trail to roughly 5,400 ft, directly west of the summit. Leave the trail here and scramble cross-country through meadows and around rock bands to gain the west ridge. From the ridge, ascend eastward toward the main summit ridge, then turn north, staying below the summit headwall, and scramble past blocky ledges (Class 2-3) to the summit pinnacle. Return the same way. ~16 miles round trip, ~5,400 ft elevation gain, 8,081 ft summit. ours.name: Mary Green Glacier (Standard Route)
ours.approach: From Holden Village (~3,300') walk the gravel road/Railroad Creek Trail (FST 1256) west about 0.9 mile to the signed junction with the Holden Lake Trail and bear right (north). The Holden Lake Trail climbs steadily for about 4 miles through forest, brush, and a few small side-creek crossings (reliable water) to Holden Lake (5,278'), set in a cirque directly below Bonanza's east face — a natural camp and last easy water before things get rougher. From the lake's outlet the tread becomes increasingly faint, skirting the north shore through slide alder and talus (real bushwhacking and route-finding here, especially early season with high water), then climbing a hillside traverse northwest to Ho
ours.descent: Reverse the route: down-climb the summit ridge and rocky rib back toward the glacier, staying climber's left of the standard line to dodge rockfall funneling down the gullies. The established descent uses 6–7 fixed rappel stations (horns, flakes, and slung boulders left by prior parties) along the class 3–4 rock band, typically consolidated into about four rappels using a 60m x 8mm rope — a common

fktText: Description Followed the standard Bonanza Peak summit route from Holden Village. Depart the village and follow forested trail to Holden Lake. Proceed past the lake and up to Holden Pass. Leave the trail here crossing water fall slabs, accessing the toe of the Mary Green Glacier. Traverse up and climbers left to access the rock. 3rd-4th class scrambling on exquisite rock brings you to the summit. More information here: https://www.summitpost.org/bonanza-peak/150586 I brought a very light rack consisting of one 19cm ice screw, a Guide ATC, a 30m / 8mm static rope for rappels, a single and a double sling, and a yellow (2) and red (1) Omega Pacific Links Cam. I had Petzl Leopard FL crampons, La Sportiva Bushido trail runners, and a Petzl Gully ice axe. I also brought along the trusty Petzl Sirocco helmet. The glacier was melted out so navigating crevasses was straightforward. Accessing the rock involved a bit of a leap over a moat, and the rock climbing itself felt solid soling. ours.name: Northeast Buttress
ours.approach: The approach follows the same trailhead-in as the standard route — Railroad Creek Trail (FST 1256) from Holden Village to the Holden Lake Trail junction, then up to Holden Lake (5,278') and Holden Pass (6,360') for high camp — but instead of angling onto the Mary Green Glacier itself, continue on benches and talus/heather to climber's right (east/north side) of the glacier. This adds roughly another 3 hours and substantial elevation gain beyond Holden Pass to reach the base of the Northeast Buttress/Face around 8,350'. ours.name: Northeast Ridge
ours.approach: From US-2 at the west end of Leavenworth, follow Icicle Road (Forest Road 7600) about 8 miles, then turn left onto the signed, gravel Eightmile Road. Cross Icicle Creek and climb about 1,100 ft to the large parking area at the road's end (passing the Eightmile Creek Trailhead en route). Northwest Forest Pass required.
ours.descent: From the summit, head to Prusik Pass and follow the standard route's trail through the Upper Enchantment Basin, down Aasgard Pass, and down the Mountaineer Creek/Colchuck Lake Trail back to the Stuart Lake Trailhead. This is a demanding ~15-mile loop with sustained class 3 scrambling and bushwhacking on the ascent, requiring at least 12 hours car-to-car and an early start.

ours.name: Chelan Butte Trail
ours.approach: From the town of Chelan, take SR 150 (E Woodin Rd), then Sanders St, Farnham St, S. Saunders St, and E. Iowa Ave to the WDFW Chelan Butte trailhead parking lot, and climb the Chelan Butte Trail directly toward the summit. Alternatively, from Highway 97A at Millard Street in Lakeside (between mileposts 232-233), follow Chelan Butte Road as it climbs the west side of the butte, staying on the road or the marked hiking-trail cutoff about 1/4 mile in.
ours.descent: Descend the same trail or road used on the way up, passing back through the Elephant Head viewpoint area to the trailhead. No technical downclimbing or rappelling is involved; watch footing on loose gravel and ruts on the road sections, especially after rain or snowmelt.

fktText: Description Run from the PUD parking lot up either the single track trail or the fall line trail to the summit. Any route can be used from the parking lot. Note our map shows the fall line trail, which is much shorter than the main trail, which has a Strava Segment . ours.name: Standard Route (Southeast Ridge via Jackita Ridge / Crater Lake Trail)
ours.approach: From the Canyon Creek Trailhead (1,900 ft) on SR 20 (32.8 mi east of Marblemount / 55.1 mi west of Winthrop), take Jackita Ridge Trail #738, crossing Granite Creek on a bridge and fording Canyon Creek near the start. The trail climbs steeply through timber via numerous switchbacks (roughly 55) gaining about 3,400 ft over 4 miles to a junction near 5,000-5,260 ft, with views opening onto Crater and Jack Mountains above timberline. Turn left onto the Crater Lake Trail (brushy, user-maintained) for about a mile to Crater Lake (about 5,800 ft) below the peak's south side.
ours.descent: From the summit, descend the scree/talus slopes back to the top of the crux gully and downclimb it carefully, following the same painted yellow X's/arrows and cairns used on the ascent (parties note this section is loose and exposure-sensitive both ways). fktText: Description From Summitpost : "Crater Mountain is a prominent peak rising north of Hwy. 20 about 5 mi. east of Ross Lake. It has deep valley footings with over 6000' of relief from the highway. Crater is the site of two former fire lookouts. One on the main summit and another on a 7054' point east of the east summit... The name "crater" probably comes from the mountain's appearance. A massive glacial cirque, holding crater lake, is carved out of the south side of the mountain. The out-of-print classic, Routes and Rocks, names the main summit of Crater as one of the five best viewpoints in the North Cascades!" Crater Mountain is an 8,132-foot (2,479-metre) mountain summit located in the North Cascades of Washington state. It is the 29th highest mountain in the Pasayten Wilderness. The mountain is well known in the area for the fun 3rd class scramble that is marked with yellow paint. Big, yellow X's and arrows guide you to the summit plateau, where you'll find remnants of an old fire lookout tower. The Mountain has an interesting history; The fire tower was built in 1932, but a camp had been established on the summit for three years prior to that. To collect water, those who worked there would have to scramble down to the Jerry Glacier on the North side of the mountain and chip off chunks of ice to be carried back up and melted in a tub in the sun. ours.name: Der Dihedral
ours.approach: Approach as for Backbone Ridge and Serpentine Arete: from the Stuart Lake Trailhead (3,400 ft) follow Stuart Lake Trail #1599 to the signed junction at 2.6 miles, then Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4.3-4.4 miles, ~2,200 ft gain, 2-2.5 hours). From the lake, follow the lateral moraine/talus below Dragontail's north face as for Backbone Ridge, but Der Dihedral's start is lower on the face and a couple of ridgelines short of (east/left of, and below) Backbone Ridge proper - it is not as well-cairned or as heavily travelled as the Backbone/Serpentine approach. fktText: Description Dragontail Peak (8840') is "A lengthy and difficult hike up an iconic peak inside the Enchantments. Climbing gear and expertise required." The route begins at the Colchuck/Stuart Lk TH, follows the trail trail to Colchuck Lake and around the south end of the lake. Climbers ascend Aasgard Pass and ascend the snowfield on the eastern slope of Dragontail to the saddle dividing the Enchantments basin to Ingalls Creek. Then ascend the ridge to the summit. It is around 13 miles TH-to-TH, with 5800+ feet of elevation gain.
